# Operating Systems and Computing Foundations

This category is about **how a computer executes, translates and represents computation**. It has three second-level subjects, as requested.

## 1. Operating System Principles

[**Operating System Principles**](operating-system-principles/index.qmd) covers processes, threads, scheduling, virtual address spaces, paging, synchronisation and deadlocks.

Start with a small question: **Two processes both use virtual address 8197. Must they access the same physical memory?** No: their separate page tables may map that same virtual address to different frames. The [paging lesson](operating-system-principles/03-virtual-memory-and-paging.qmd) explains this with real numbers.

## 2. Compiler Principles

[**Compiler Principles**](compiler-principles/index.qmd) explains lexical analysis, parsing, type checking, abstract syntax trees, intermediate representation, SSA and safe optimisation.

Start with the expression \`2+3*4\`. The [parsing lesson](compiler-principles/01-lexing-and-parsing.qmd) shows why the answer is 14 rather than 20, by turning the string into a tree that reflects the grammar.

## 3. Quantum Computing

[**Quantum Computing**](quantum-computing/index.qmd) is included here as a separately labelled, interdisciplinary computing topic. It is **not a subfield of classical operating-system design**; it connects computation to linear algebra and quantum physics.

Begin with a qubit, measurement and a Hadamard gate. Then study two-qubit entanglement and interference in circuits. The examples distinguish *mathematical ideal-state predictions* from noisy hardware observations.

## Our teaching contract

Every chapter follows the same path: **one problem → intuition → mathematical relationship → definitions of every symbol → numbers substituted → explanation → counterexample or limitation.**

There are no empty chapter pages in this first instalment. We will expand this structure gradually with deeper topics and original experiments.

## Original verification lab

[Use the small independent lab](examples/index.qmd) to check the arithmetic behind the scheduling, paging, parsing and quantum probability examples. It uses only Python's standard library; a full OS, LLVM installation or quantum SDK is unnecessary to verify these particular numbers.

**Reference families:** [Linux kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/), [LLVM tutorial](https://llvm.org/docs/tutorial/MyFirstLanguageFrontend/), and [IBM Quantum Learning](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en).
